title: Say the good thing
instruction: Notice one thing they handled today that you would normally leave unspoken. Tell them you noticed.
why_it_matters: Effort is easy to stop noticing when you see it every day. Saying it out loud brings it back into view.

title: Catch the autopilot
instruction: Pick one routine moment you usually do on autopilot. Watch what each of you does, and name the pattern privately to yourself.
why_it_matters: You can change a routine more easily once you notice the exact moment it takes over.

title: One real follow-up
instruction: Ask one genuine follow-up question about something your partner tells you today before sharing your own story.
why_it_matters: A real follow-up shows that you are still with them instead of waiting for your turn.

title: A warmer hello
instruction: When you first see each other today, stop what you're doing and greet them with a form of touch that is already normal and welcome between you. Let it last one extra beat.
why_it_matters: A familiar hello can become invisible. Giving it a little more warmth makes the reunion feel intentional again.

title: Catch the story
instruction: Catch one annoyed thought about your partner today. Name the story your mind is telling you before you react.
why_it_matters: The first explanation in your head is not always the only one. Catching it gives you room to choose your response.

title: Find one detail
instruction: Notice one detail about your partner you haven't paid attention to lately: their clothes, expression, music, food choice, or something they're absorbed in.
why_it_matters: Familiarity can narrow attention. Deliberately noticing detail makes the familiar visible again.

title: Ask beyond logistics
instruction: Ask your partner one question today that has nothing to do with schedules, chores, money, food, or plans.
why_it_matters: A question outside logistics gives you something to talk about besides managing the day.

title: Catch the bid
instruction: Catch one brief attempt your partner makes to connect: a joke, photo, comment, question, or look. Give it a real response.
why_it_matters: Connection often starts in brief moments. Responding tells your partner that their attempt reached you.

title: Remember what drew you in
instruction: Bring to mind one thing that first drew you to your partner. Tell them, or simply carry it with you the next time you see them.
why_it_matters: Remembering what first attracted you can bring back a version of your partner that daily logistics often hide.

title: Five minutes, no admin
instruction: Spend five minutes together without talking about chores, schedules, work admin, or tomorrow's plans.
why_it_matters: Briefly removing logistical talk creates room for a different kind of interaction.

title: Take a new route
instruction: Take a walk together and choose streets you've never walked down before. No destination needed. Just explore for ten minutes.
why_it_matters: A different route gives you something new to notice together without needing a plan.

title: Choose for each other
instruction: Get a coffee, snack, or treat together and choose for each other. Keep it within things you already know the other person likes.
why_it_matters: A low-stakes change to a familiar choice introduces novelty and attention without requiring a special date.

title: Send the unexpected thing
instruction: Send them something during the day that isn't practical: a photo, thought, joke, or something that made you think of them.
why_it_matters: Changing a communication channel from coordination to connection adds novelty to an ordinary day.

title: Hand over one choice
instruction: Give your partner one choice you usually make today: the music, route, show, dinner, or where you sit. Go with their pick.
why_it_matters: Letting them choose changes the usual rhythm and gives you a chance to follow instead of lead.

title: Unexpected favor
instruction: Do one useful or enjoyable thing they aren't expecting today. Keep it easy enough that it doesn't create an obligation to react.
why_it_matters: An unexpected favor says 'I was thinking about you' without asking for anything back.

title: Try their pick
instruction: Choose one low-stakes thing your partner likes that you usually wouldn't pick: a song, snack, short video, route, or activity. Join them in it once.
why_it_matters: Joining something they like lets you meet them inside their world for a moment.

title: Add ten minutes
instruction: Turn one errand together into ten extra minutes. Walk another block, sit somewhere, or wander into a place you've never stopped at.
why_it_matters: Adding time to something you already had to do creates shared time without planning a separate date.

title: Sit a little closer
instruction: During one ordinary moment together, sit close enough for comfortable contact for a minute. Use the kind of closeness that is already normal and welcome between you.
why_it_matters: Familiar, welcome touch can add warmth to an ordinary moment without turning it into a big gesture.

title: Bring back a song
instruction: Play one song connected to a good shared memory. Ask what they remember about that time.
why_it_matters: A familiar song can pull an old shared moment back into the room and give you something real to talk about.

title: Let the phone wait
instruction: Choose one ordinary five-minute moment together today and leave your phone out of reach until the moment is over.
why_it_matters: Putting the phone out of reach makes attention easier because you do not have to keep choosing against it.

title: Invite them along
instruction: Invite your partner into one thing you'd normally do alone today: a walk, shop run, coffee, cooking, or quick errand.
why_it_matters: An invitation turns an existing routine into an opportunity for shared activity without adding much effort.

title: Say what you still like
instruction: Tell your partner one thing you still like about who they are. Make it about them, not a chore or favor they did.
why_it_matters: Being valued for who you are feels different from being thanked for what you do.

title: Reverse one role
instruction: For one routine today, swap who normally does it or who takes the lead.
why_it_matters: Swapping a familiar role can show you what the other person normally carries without much discussion.

title: Ask for a micro-adventure
instruction: Offer two easy options that are different from the usual: walk after dinner or dessert outside, new café or old favorite. Let them pick.
why_it_matters: Constrained choices make novelty easier to act on than vague plans to 'do more together.'

title: Change the first minute
instruction: Pick one recurring moment today: waking up, coming home, dinner, getting into the car. Deliberately change only its first minute.
why_it_matters: Changing the first minute can stop the rest of a familiar moment from running exactly the usual way.

title: Add one playful choice
instruction: Turn one boring decision today into a playful one: coin flip the takeaway, each pick a mystery snack, or choose the next song for each other.
why_it_matters: A playful choice gives an ordinary decision a different energy.

title: Pause one beat
instruction: Take one breath before answering the first time you feel a sharp, dismissive, or impatient reply coming.
why_it_matters: One breath is often enough to stop the first sharp reply from deciding the rest of the exchange.

title: What else could it mean?
instruction: Catch one moment when you decide what your partner meant. Ask yourself, “What else could this mean?” before responding.
why_it_matters: The first meaning you give a comment is not always the only one. Another plausible reading can change your next response.

title: Finish hearing it
instruction: Let your partner fully finish one story or point today before you start preparing your answer.
why_it_matters: Letting them finish makes listening the main task for a moment, rather than preparing your reply.

title: Answer the feeling first
instruction: Respond to the feeling first when your partner tells you about something frustrating today. Leave advice and fixing for later.
why_it_matters: People often want to feel understood before they want a solution.

title: Say it softer
instruction: Say one difficult point in a calmer first sentence today. Keep the point; change the delivery.
why_it_matters: Changing delivery while keeping the underlying need intact tests whether the interaction pattern can shift without avoidance.

title: Repair the miss
instruction: Repair one miss as soon as you notice it. Say, “That came out wrong,” or “Sorry, I wasn't listening,” and try the moment again.
why_it_matters: A quick repair can stop one bad moment from becoming the tone of the next ten minutes.

title: Make one clean request
instruction: Turn one “Why do you always...?” thought into a concrete request about what you need right now.
why_it_matters: A specific request reduces mind-reading and global judgments while preserving the underlying need.

title: Drop the scoreboard once
instruction: Catch yourself mentally counting who did more once today. Decide what you need, then ask for it plainly or let this one go.
why_it_matters: Moving from internal scorekeeping to a specific choice interrupts resentment-building without denying genuine imbalance.

title: Bring back your shared humor
instruction: Bring one piece of shared humor into an ordinary moment today: an old callback, a silly voice, a meme, or a joke you both already like.
why_it_matters: Shared humor can interrupt a serious, practical rhythm and remind you that the two of you have more than one way of being together.

title: Turn toward
instruction: Give your partner your full attention for ten seconds the next time they show you something or make a brief comment. Then return to what you were doing.
why_it_matters: Giving one moment your full attention makes it clear that what they said reached you.

title: Ask before fixing
instruction: Ask, “Do you want ideas or do you want me to listen?” the first time your partner brings you a problem today.
why_it_matters: A simple choice interrupts habitual fixing and makes support more responsive to what is actually wanted.

title: Reset outside
instruction: Take a ten-minute walk together when the mood at home feels stuck. Leave the problem indoors for the first five minutes.
why_it_matters: A change of setting can loosen a mood that has started to feel stuck.

title: A warmer goodbye
instruction: Before one separation today, make the goodbye warmer than usual. Use a form of affection that is already normal and welcome between you, then name one thing you're looking forward to later.
why_it_matters: A warmer goodbye gives an ordinary transition some attention and creates a reason to look forward to reconnecting.

title: Rewrite the first reply
instruction: Rewrite one irritated text before sending it. Remove the sentence you wouldn't say calmly face-to-face.
why_it_matters: Text makes sharp first reactions easy to send. Rewriting once gives the calmer version a chance.

title: Pick one keeper
instruction: Choose one Move from the last three weeks that genuinely improved a moment between you. Mark that one as worth repeating.
why_it_matters: Selecting a behavior that produced a useful result makes repetition intentional rather than relying on memory.

title: Attach it to a cue
instruction: Take one Keeper and decide exactly when it will happen again: after coffee, when you get home, on the walk to the shop, or before sleep.
why_it_matters: Putting a Keeper after something you already do makes it easier to remember.

title: Make it smaller
instruction: Take a Move you liked but found hard to repeat. Reduce it until it feels almost too easy to skip: twenty minutes becomes five; a big plan becomes one question.
why_it_matters: Reducing friction makes repetition more likely and helps separate the useful behavior from unnecessary effort.

title: Repeat the warmer hello
instruction: Repeat the warmer hello from earlier in the Routine: stop, look up, and use a form of touch that is already normal and welcome between you.
why_it_matters: Repeating the same warm hello helps it become part of how you reconnect.

title: Protect five minutes
instruction: Choose one five-minute window that worked well for you: coffee, after dinner, a walk, before bed. Make it deliberately phone-free again today.
why_it_matters: Protecting the same five minutes again makes focused time easier to repeat.

title: Keep the outside ritual
instruction: Pick one outside ritual you could realistically repeat weekly: a walk, coffee stop, market lap, bench, or errand detour. Do it or choose when you'll do it next.
why_it_matters: Attaching connection to an existing place or routine lowers the effort needed to repeat it.

title: Keep the question
instruction: Choose one question that opened a better conversation this month. Ask it again in a new context rather than searching for a brand-new technique.
why_it_matters: A question that worked once is worth using again. Familiarity can make good conversation easier, not less meaningful.

title: Plan for the bad day
instruction: Choose one Keeper and finish this sentence privately: 'Even on a busy or bad day, I can still do the two-minute version by…'
why_it_matters: Planning a minimum version protects a new behavior when motivation and time are low.

title: Make the cue visible
instruction: For one Keeper, change the environment so it reminds you: put the phones away at dinner, leave walking shoes by the door, or add a private calendar cue.
why_it_matters: A visible reminder means the Keeper does not depend on remembering at exactly the right moment.

title: Name what changed
instruction: Tonight, name one interaction that feels different from four weeks ago and the behavior that helped change it.
why_it_matters: Naming what changed helps you see which behaviors are actually worth keeping.
